utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Just very briefly, I see that Mr. Moore is waiting address the Court as well before the witness is brought in. There is one concern that I would like to express. Just this morning we received an addendum to the statement of the witness who is about to appear. It appears to be quite important. I think our questions will reflect that, and also the Prosecutor's questions concerning all the new things that the witness has now added to his statement. As for my concern, however, and I informed Mr. Moore that I would be informing you, we see that the OTP interviewed the 19th of May about this addendum. We only got this this morning at 10.00. I think this severely prejudiced us in preparing our cross-examination of this witness. That is what I wish to inform you about. We are not applying for any sort of deferral at all, but I think it would only be fair to be given this sort of addendum at the time the witness actually signs it. I think we should have been informed ahead of time. That's all I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's correct, the witness was seen on the 19th of May. It is one page, it deals with nine points. Major Sljivancanin's name is mentioned once, the other defendants are not mentioned. It deals with two or individuals, principally, Vukasinovic and Karanfilov. It's not if possible to transcribe documents like this immediately. The next time that we were able to see the witness was yesterday when we were here, or I was here. He read it, he agreed it, and he signed it. And that was the first time that it could then be released because we were not able to have it signed before then. And with the utmost respect to my learned friend, it is not a major area of concern. It deals with areas of evidence that the Court have already heard about. There is nothing new about this. It deals about incidents at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber, of course, does not see this, so it doesn't know for itself at the moment what it is that has been exchanged. Thank you, Mr. Moore. Was there some other matter, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, there is no other matter at all. We are ready to call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the witness then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: To assist the Court, this witness has voice distortion and image distortion, and I regrettably will have to make an application for much of his evidence to be in private session. The nature of the evidence that he gives would lead to his ready identification. However, I can deal with the first part in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I wonder, Witness, if you would kind enough, please, to look at these personal details and confirm that they are accurate.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I make application that they be made an exhibit under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be exhibit number 557, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I ask now to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, is this a prolonged proposal or for a short time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The curriculum vitae, the background, would be in private, and there are parts of his evidence that would make him readily identifiable. And I will try and ensure that his evidence is in open session as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness 001, I would like to now ask you, through your time of service in Vukovar, did you at any time go to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What were the circumstances of you going to Ovcara, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I went to Ovcara under the following circumstances: There was a certain number of prisoners, members of the ZNG, and the situation was an unstable one, a critical one. I, and members of my unit, were to do our best and ensure that the prisoners are protected and later on I guess transported to certain military institutions or prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We believe that the fall of Vukovar was the 18th of November. If one uses that as a yard-stick, are you able to say when it was you received that contact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: That was two days later on the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So how many people actually went with you to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: My rough estimate is eight to 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Had you ever participated in a role before where you were asked to intervene in a difficult situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes. That was sometime before the final fighting, when a group of volunteers refused to carry out commands and participate in combat, expressing their desire to go back, or rather to desert the combat area. However, they wanted to leave the area with their equipment and weapons. There was a need to intervene urgently, because they were being -- expressing lack of subordination. I met with several commanders -- I intercepted a group with a group of commanders, and I immediately made it known to them that I would accept no insubordination. That was between Negoslavci and Vukovar, on the road between those two places. I forced them to discard all of their weapons and equipment and then we proceeded to frisk them. While doing that we found on them a certain amount of money, jewellery. Then we turned them over to the command in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you went to Ovcara, how long did it take you to arrive from your location to actually Ovcara itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Some 20 minutes. 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you arrived at Ovcara, what did you find, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: It was night-time. Could have been sometime between 9.00 and 10.00 p.m. By the hangar -- or, rather, we stopped by the hangar and I saw the lights of a bus which were turned on. I came out and I saw Major Vukasinovic who right then told me that I should stay there and ensure that the prisoners, whom I later saw in the hangar, are safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How did you actually get there? Did you walk or did you go by vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: We drove with our vehicles. That is to say our jeeps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us that you stopped at the hangar and you were told to stay there. How long did you actually remain at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: In my view, 15 to 20 minutes, give or take a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see any other officer that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I also saw Captain Karanfilov.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you able to see what was happening in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes. When I looked inside through the open door, I saw on the right side, on the right from the entrance door, a group of people with terrified expressions on their faces. They stood about one metre away from a rope, which was tied from one end -- from one wall to the other one. What remained vividly in my mind was a stench that was most likely the result of enormous fear. Members of my unit started entering the hangar, I told them to come out. And at that point we came out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you eventually leave the hangar area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes. We came out, and then for some time we stood outside of the hangar, in front of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did anyone speak to you about whether you should stay or remain? Stay or leave, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Major Vukasinovic did. He gave me orders to -- he gave me orders stating that there was no longer any need for us to be there, and that we could go back to where we had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal with the people that you saw inside. How would you describe their demeanour at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Their conduct was typical for people whose fate, or rather whose life at that point in time are absolutely beyond their control. There was a lot of fear, tremendous fear that one could see on the faces of these people. There was some sort of a lamp shedding light on their faces, so their expressions were quite visible. It was a humiliating expression that they had on their faces which, I guess, is common among people who are imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you were ordered by Major Vukasinovic that there was no reason for you to remain, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: We got back into our jeeps and we started driving back towards Vukovar. That is to say, back towards the high school building in Vukovar where part of my unit was to spend the night that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you were in the area of Ovcara and the hangar, did you hear any other noises?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: As we were travelling back towards the high school, towards Vukovar, I heard fire shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I've heard "fire shots" in translation. Is that the same as firing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you able to say how close that firing was to the hangar at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Not precisely, but judging by the intensity, I would say that it was a matter of several hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour give me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever know the leader of a TO unit with the name of Stanko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Visually, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you know him before the 20th of November? When I say "know," I mean visually know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever know a leader of a TO unit called Miroljub?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you get to know him after the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you went to the hangar for that brief period, did you see either of those two gentlemen at the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal then, please, with one or two other areas of your evidence. Do you know an officer called Captain Papic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you ever had any conversation with Papic about the matters at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you remember when you had a conversation with Papic about what occurred at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: That was a conversation held at a canteen when we were having breakfast. That was in early 1992. At that time he spoke about the bodies which were covered with soil by bulldozers. He was a commander of a mechanised unit, and he said that his equipment and his people took part in burying bodies at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did Papic indicate what he felt when he was obliged to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes. He felt sickened by it. That was the dominant sentiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to move to a different topic, if I may, please. Do you know or did you know in 1991 an officer called Borisavljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you have any conversation with Borisavljevic about incidents that occurred at the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what was said, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I apologise. Borisavljevic told me the following: Once the combat ceased in Vukovar and when armed resistance ceased, some of the prisoners were put in the Vukovar barracks. He was in charge of them. At one point in time a man called Zeljko Raznjatovic, nicknamed Arkan, appeared. At the time he was known as the commander of the Serb volunteer guard. He demanded that he turn over the group of prisoners to him. Since Borisavljevic declined to do that, Arkan was visibly upset, and he threatened him, saying that he would nevertheless have to hand them over. Another incident that he told me about was the event in a facility called Velepromet. One night he was summoned there, and when he arrived he saw guards, ordinary JNA soldiers, but members of the military police who were there as guards, guarding the people at Velepromet. He saw several corpses, bloody walls, and traces on bodies indicating that they were fired at from a fire-arm at close range. This is what Borisavljevic told me about these two instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is it right that you have subsequently left Serbia - I think it was in 1996 - and you are now a resident in another country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Just a second, please. Good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I need to ask you something. Since both of us speak the same language, I would like to ask you to make a short break before answering my questions. There are two reasons for that. One is that you are a protected witness, and we shouldn't let your voice escape through my microphone. The other reason is to give a chance to interpreters to interpret my questions and your answers so that everybody can follow our dialogue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I will continue where my learned friend left it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And perhaps we should go into private session at this point, because this has to do precisely with the circumstances surrounding the departure of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, in view of the ruling of the Trial Chamber to set aside two weeks in order to bring in expert witnesses who should be present when Mr. Theunens testifies, that would bring us to the 19th that my learned friend mentioned, and that date would be fine with the Defence. I believe we should be able to organise everything needed for our expert witnesses. As for the other questions you put, Your Honours, as to the length of cross-examination, I can't give you any estimates right now. As for Mr. Theunens, his expert report has several hundred pages dealing with the position and the role of the Yugoslav People's Army, which might be interesting for us in view of its role in the geographic area from our indictment. The other part of the report deals with the specific orders issued by the 1st Military District and the guards brigade. The only thing we can promise you is that the Defence will try to be as efficient as possible. However, we have to cover with this expert witness some issues that he wrote about but are not directly emanating from the text of the law. There are certain portions where our opinions differ in relation to that and in relation to some orders. As for Mr. Pringle, I think the situation is even more complex, because this expert witness provides his view of the situation linked to our indictment which does not arise directly from the documentation as is the case with Mr. Theunens. Now, Mr. Kostovic. As my learned friend said, there will be some issues that are disputed concerning some documents, MFI documents, precisely because the Defence asked to be allowed to challenge some of the facts mentioned there. We received some documents relating to Mr. Kostovic's testimony, and we will deal only with those which we find contentious. These are documents provided by Dr. Vesna Bosanac. I can't tell you exactly how many such issues there are, but I can promise you that we will only deal with those that are contentious in the sense that they are not in compliance with some of our other documents. I don't know if my other colleagues wish to contribute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will be very brief. I fully support the efforts of the Trial Chamber to ensure that the trial proceeds smoothly and efficiently. I believe it to be in everybody's interests, especially in the interests of my client. However, it would be good if the Prosecution would tell us exactly who their witnesses are before expert witnesses. P-002 doesn't seem to be an important witness to me, but if the Prosecution believes they are they should have mentioned this earlier. We spoke about this a week or two ago. If this witness is now certain to come then, once again, we find ourselves in the situation where we do not know whether it's P-002 coming or Grujic coming on Monday. So we would like for the Trial Chamber to instruct the Prosecution to tell us definitely who is coming and when. The Defence of Miroslav Radic will accept any schedule, even their proposed schedule for expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As I understand it, Mr. Borovic, there will be one witness after the present this week, then Mr. Grujic next Monday, and perhaps Tuesday, with 002 to follow that. And then we get to the week of Monday, the 21st of -- Monday, the 19th of June. Now, for cross-examination of Theunens, Pringle and Kostovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What Mr. Vasic said would suit us best; namely, for the 19th of June to be set aside as the time for expert witnesses. As for the Defence of Radic, it is not necessary for us even to bring in our expert witnesses, but we will need the time up to the 19th to prepare. And we will not require much time for cross-examination. That is to say, we will comply with all of your previous instructions on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. And Mr. Lukic always tries to comply as well, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, if that is a compliment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a prayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you are probably most interested in is the cross-examination, the length of it when it comes to expert witnesses. I am afraid that the cross-examination of such important witnesses such as Theunens and Pringle should not be limited in advance. I will, however, propose that you do something that you haven't done so far, namely, if you find that some of the questions go beyond the proper scope of cross-examination and that they are not relevant, I would suggest that you instruct us accordingly to limit our cross-examination. However, I find that I am unable to say that we will need an hour or two for these expert witnesses. I would rather opt for this other option where you tell us which questions you find irrelevant. I think that these are very important witnesses and that we will comply with whatever is instructed. As for our expert witnesses, we will ensure that they are present, and I don't think that there will be a problem there, since we have two weeks to organise that. As for Kostovic, I think we agreed that his statement can be admitted into evidence. And, just as Mrs. Tapuskovic did on Friday, we will try to go by numbers and try to not make it too complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I be more specific then, for Defence counsel: Is it a practical idea to think that if the Prosecution took no more than one session with Mr. Kostovic and no more than a session and a half with both Mr. Theunens and Mr. Pringle that Mr. Kostovic could be finished in one sitting day and Mr. Theunens and Mr. Pringle in two days. That would give altogether for cross-examination about four and a half hours of each of Theunens and Pringle. That way the three witnesses could be completed Monday to Friday when your experts are available.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have not spoken among ourselves, I can just give you my position. Unless we have the long sitting hours, I don't think that we should have enough time. I think all of us should have the same amount of time as the Prosecution takes in examination-in-chief. We can do our best, but I really fear that it will be counter-productive to limit our time in advance. I can promise you we will do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sitting days on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday of that week. And that would actually give you longer than we were proposing to limit the Prosecution to, you see. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would just like to amplify what Mr. Lukic said to show you what the view of the Defence is. Mr. Kostovic was asked to come to testify precisely in order to clarify the problems that were found in the documents provided by Dr. Bosanac. So his role is simply to clarify these differences that exist, and we will focus exclusively on that. As for experts Pringle and Theunens, I understand that it will be enough for the Prosecution to have just one session or a session and a half, because they will tender into evidence thousands of pages via expert reports. But I am afraid that the Defence will need to cover report perhaps not in its entirety, but at least to cover the issues that we find contentious. So perhaps the proper way to limit this would be to ensure that none of the questions are irrelevant and that they stay well within the proper scope of examination-in-chief. Perhaps that would be the best way rather than set a strict time limit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I know that sounds more attractive to you, Mr. Vasic, but it has the disadvantage that you might plan to cross-examine for six days and then leave it to us to try and say no, that question is no good, this question is no good. Whereas if you planned to cross-examine for a fixed time you yourself will get to the matters that are more important. We are trying to ensure that you have time to deal with the important issues. We have never, I hope, limited your time so that you have not been able to do that. Only Mr. Lukic has suffered, being at the tail-end once or twice, I fear. But, that aside, we have tried to give you full time to deal with what is important. That time may not always have been well used, but nevertheless it was there. And so just to say, well, look, if we think something is too far out we'll stop you, we really don't know what it is that's very important that's still to come. You know yourself what you want to cover, so you are the best person to work out what is the most important and to concentrate on that. Thank you, then, for your assistance. Mr. Moore, is there anything further?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The only other matter, because that would conclude the case. The only other matter will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Oh, on that topic, no, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you've got another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's really for Mr. Lukic. There are certain interviews that the defendants participated in in Belgrade. It was going to be our application that they are admissable. I think it's right to say that Mr. Lukic takes the view that they are inadmissible. We need to clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Interviewed conducted by?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Interviews conducted by, I think, the military court when the defendants were witnesses, made certain observations and comments. We will be submitting that it is admissable and therefore should be evidence before the Court. My learned friend Mr. Lukic, I think, has submissions to the contrary. That has to be clarified. Mr. Lukic is aware of it. It's not the case that the Defence have been caught unawares. Perhaps he and I can discuss the matter outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, if that needs to be the subject of submissions, they can be put briefly, I'm sure, and by the look of it, there could be time even later this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. So you can look forward to that, Mr. Lukic. The Chamber will consider just what to do and perhaps before the end of today let you know about the position of these coming witnesses. Now, Mr. Moore, you need your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, if he could be recalled, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May I indicate while we wait for the witness that the view of the Chamber is that it should indicate that it would want to hear the three experts in the week commencing the 19th of June. And to that end the evidence in chief of Kostovic should not exceed one session, and the evidence in chief of both Theunens and Pringle should not exceed one and a half sessions each. And the Defence then will have the balance of that time. And certainly with Kostovic, if he can be finished in less than a day, because there really are only a number of specific issues, that would allow more time for the other two experts. If you could mention that to your colleagues, Mr. Moore, so that we can have a speedy examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. Can we please go back into private session to complete the topic that we began before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you agree that at this time there were no contacts between members of the guards brigade and members of Goran Hadzic's government either?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I don't know about that. It's not my place to speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the HQ of the Serb volunteers' guard on the one hand and the government seat on the other were both in Erdut, north of Vukovar, that was in the area covered by Operations Group North, the Novi Sad corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: You are suggesting that the headquarters of the Serb volunteers' guard was in Erdut, which at the same time was used as a training camp. I did know about that. I was also aware of the fact that it was the Novi Sad corps that was responsible for this sector. As for the government of the Eastern Slavonia region or whatever it was called at the time being in Dalj, now this is not something that I knew about at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You mentioned your conversation with Captain Cedo Papic back in 1992. He was commander of the engineers' company. Do you remember mentioning this to the OTP investigators when you provided your statement? Just a minute, please. I'm not sure if the witness thinks this should be stricken, what I have just mentioned in my question. If so, I'm sure we can oblige. Then we should go into private session. If not, we can just continue in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I believe you can continue, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember Mr. Papic saying that some members of his company were burying bodies at Ovcara near Vukovar and that bodies were being brought there uninterruptedly during the fighting? Do you remember telling the OTP investigators about this, or perhaps you need to go back to your statement to see what exactly it says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: If you are referring to a specific portion of the statement, could you please provide a reference for me, page and paragraph, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: By all means. I'm talking about your statement to the OTP, the page number is 9, the B/C/S ERN is 0304-7041. The English reference, for the benefit of my learned friends ... I see that my learned friend has found it already. I thank him for this speedy reaction. Sir, this is paragraph 2 from the bottom of the page up. Isn't this what you stated to the OTP investigators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: You're quite welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You discuss events which you claim occurred at Velepromet. Would you agree with me that throughout the fighting and after the fighting Velepromet was under the control of Vukovar's TO and that the person in charge of Velepromet was Mr. Ljubinko Stojanovic, later to become director of Radio Vukovar. At the time he was assistant commander of the Vukovar TO staff. You did say so to the investigators, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. But if I remember correctly I also said the following: That Velepromet was used for the accommodation of civilians, and according to my information people of Serb ethnicity were registered and transported to Serbia while non-Serb civilians were kept there and used for forced labour. That part of the statement, and I can mention the family Crnobrnja there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Today for the first time you mentioned Ovcara in the context that you mentioned it in. Since we are in open session, I'm not going to deal with any details. I would just like to ask you what you would say if I were to tell you that the events you talked about were actually two days before than you say, and that people from that unit say that that was on the 18th of November, 1991, and not on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: The date as a temporal indicator of events is something that I could have mentioned, but according to what I remember it's the 20th. However, please don't hold me strictly to the dates, because then I take upon myself the risk of being mistaken about the date. So I do accept the possibility. If it is established specifically that it was the 18th, I accept that as a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir, for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, my name is Borivoje Borovic. I am an attorney from Belgrade, and I am defending Miroslav Radic. In response to the Prosecutor's question you mentioned the Territorial Defence in Vukovar. In that context, you mentioned the 1st Assault Detachment. You didn't tell us if you know who commanded the 1st Assault Detachment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I wasn't asked, and now that you ask me, I can say that the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment was Major Tesic. Right now I cannot remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were at Ovcara and irrespective of the date, do you know who the commander was of the Ovcara location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find out later, because reading the statement you gave to the OTP I see that you conducted some investigations about these events. So did you find out who was the local commander of Ovcara at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I didn't find out that particular thing, and I wasn't really interested in who the commander was. What I did find out and what I do know is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether you knew who the commander was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you said that you know Stanko in response to a question by the Prosecutor. My question is: Is this Stanko Vujanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that to the left of you, along the axis of attack, that's where he was; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you say "to the left of you," in the course of operations during combat operations, do you know which company was also on that axis of attack to the left of you? Specifically was it Captain Bojkovski's company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I had two neighbours in two periods of time that I was there. In the first period it was the right flank of the 1st Assault Detachment, and it's possible that that was Captain Bojkovski's company, but in any case it was a company of the 1st Assault Detachment. In the second phase of my stay there, there was a company of the battalion of the military police from Avala.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that Stanko operated along the axis of operation of the company of Captain Bojkovski, or actually what is Captain Bojkovic today?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And that is -- that pertains to that time when you said that he was to the left of you. Excuse me, there is a mistake in the transcript. On page 45, line 18, the Witness said battalion and here it says battery. No, no, it's correct now. It's correct now. It does say battalion. Thank you very much. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Stanko was to the left of my position with his group and behind me. He was on my left flank and behind me. His specific combat action on that section of the front is something that I cannot speak about, because I didn't know that personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Specifically to the left of you was the company of Captain Bojkovski; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please now have Exhibit 171 on the monitors? It's just a short video film footage and I would like to ask the witness to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you see it on your screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: No, not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see what it says at the beginning of this little film? If not, maybe we can play it again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you kindly tell the Trial Chamber what it says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: "100 Days of Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who this is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: The person that I saw is Captain Bojkovski. It's the person with the walkie-talkie in his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber exactly what this person is saying? [Videotape played].

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes, I can. "Taxi, Vukovar must fall tonight. Let us move on."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Stanko Vujanovic was nicknamed "Taxi."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: No. All I know is that he was a taxi driver before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We won't need this exhibit anymore. I just wanted the Trial Chamber to have confirmation who this exactly is, because before it was just my word. Do you know the axis of operation of the 2nd Assault Detachment and who commanded the 2nd Assault Detachment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Major Adem Bajic was the commander of the 2nd Assault Detachment. And the 2nd Assault Detachment advanced along the axis through Sajmiste, which is where I was. I was actually on the left flank of the 2nd Assault Detachment between those two detachments. And its right flank was also carrying out operations in the direction of the settlement called Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree that this was also the direction of the barracks towards the water-tower? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And does that mean that there were two different directions of the 1st Assault Detachment and the 2nd Assault Detachment, they did not operate on the same axis? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: It seems logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement to the Prosecution on page 5, line 4, and if necessary you will look at it, you said that the Vukovar front in October 1991, was visited by General Adzic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You also said that he toured the positions of the 2nd Assault Detachment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was the barracks at that time the place where the command was of the 2nd Assault Detachment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When General Adzic came were you there, yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I personally did not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: However?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: However, I saw his escort, members of the same detachment that was taken out of my or our composition and attached to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that General Adzic had his own security and that when he was visiting any unit, especially at the front, this unit had to guard him? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes. In principle that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That day he was in Vukovar, like you said, at positions of the 2nd Assault Detachment. Do you know how long he stayed there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know where he went after leaving the positions of the 2nd Assault Detachment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: No, I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise, I cannot see the transcript, so I don't know if I'm going too fast or not. This is just an observation, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 48, line 19, the answer was not registered, "exclusively his security." I just wanted to mention that for the transcript. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My next question, sir. On the 19th of November, were you in Vukovar? This is in 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I can say with a great degree of certainty, yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember where you were that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I cannot specifically say where I was. I know that that day or the day before or the day after, I was busy with a crew of Sky News. I was facilitating their work as journalists, amongst other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to be completely specific. From the 18th until the 20th, did you go to the Vukovar Hospital at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were you in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: No, I did not enter the hospital building itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us who was guarding the hospital from the outside when you went there, if you saw that? Which units were involved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: It could have only have been the 1st Assault Detachment or units that were a part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you heard of Captain Simic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I cannot remember Captain Simic right this minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that he was a commander of the military police company, would that help you at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: From which battalion? There were two battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of the military police company at all, and did you know that military police company was guarding facilities and buildings and performing activities in compliance with the law?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I don't understand, which military police company? Which military police company are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you were in front of the hospital, did you see any military police at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I cannot answer your question with any degree of certainty, positively, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see soldiers with white cross belts guarding the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes, there were some people like that. There were many journalists, soldiers, a convoy was getting ready with buses, but I cannot be more specific, unfortunately, about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to tell you that Captain Simic with his company of the military police was actually guarding the hospital, would you agree with that, that he was in charge of that, if I were to tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... how can the witness answer that if he cannot remember who Captain Simic is. The answer at 53:6 is, "I cannot remember Captain Simic right at this minute."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told the witness, if I were to tell you that Captain Simic and his military police company were guarding the hospital, does that mean that you allow for that possibility, since you don't know who the soldiers with the white cross belts, which units actually they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I cannot answer something that is being put forward as a possibility. Of course there is that possibility. The building was at that point in time secured by a certain company of the military police, but I cannot tell you whether -- that that was really so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So you don't know the unit that was securing the hospital, which military police company it belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you speak to General Vasiljevic after the war in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: About Vukovar or in Vukovar? What was your question exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: About Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where and when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically the time; however, I know that it was at the time where -- when General Vasiljevic had left the prison. I went to visit him at his house several times. I wanted to express my support. And naturally I wanted to see him. Therefore, it is possible that it was during those visits that we discussed Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was anybody else present when the two of you met?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Mostly, no. Except or one occasion when a former security officer was present. I would rather not mention the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't have to mention the name. Did General Vasiljevic ever introduce you to a journalist? A civilian journalist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Actually, yes. It wasn't a typical introduction, more of an informal type.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So you sat in the presence of which person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Occasionally I would meet with a journalist whose name is Milos Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is that the journalist employed by the Vreme magazine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes, he was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Why did you meet with him, if it's not a secret? Why did you meet with a journalist of Vreme, and several times too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: It's no secret at all. At the time I had a different orientation, and I met with some people whom I didn't know in my previous life. We mostly discussed the events surrounding the break-up of our former country. We also discussed the war and also since at the time we were already following Radio Free Europe, we could hear certain pieces of information which one couldn't hear on the strictly censored television programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Was that the journalist that General Vasiljevic introduced you to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes, and I've replied that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did he introduce you to another journalist of Vreme, another person employed by Vreme at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I used to meet other journalists as well, independently of General Vasiljevic. I also met a journalist whose name was Filip Svarm, who also worked for Vreme. We met in a bar on one occasion, and that was a lady journalist, the correspondent of Financial Times. That's what I can remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever meet the journalist Jovan Dulovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I can't remember the name, but it is possible that we met. Because in those meetings usually several people would be present, and I would talk to several people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was it during your visits or meetings with General Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that it was then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: I can't say, I can't give you a definitive answer, and I would rather not guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever heard of Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear what the witness answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear your answer. Did you say yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So you are confirming that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did he have a reputation of a brave and honest officer who complied with the discipline rules of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: Among other things, yes. Because those who were members of the guards brigade were selected for that unit precisely based on those criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Since you were there at the front, did you hear there some information about him being a proper, decent officer? Was he a brave man, an honest man who abided by all the discipline rules, or did you perhaps hear something bad about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001
utterances.text: During the combat it was said that precisely what you just mentioned was true. Also, in relation to Major Sljivancanin, that members of his unit fought bravely and that he was very good in carrying out the tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have concluded your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. It's clearly time now for the second break. We will resume at 10 minutes past 4.00. Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission. Your Honours, the Defence of Major Sljivancanin has a favour to ask. We heard from our learned friend, Mr. Moore, today that the addendum provided by this witness doesn't have any important elements, and that it's not so important. We, however, believe that it's very important for Mr. Sljivancanin, because this is something that this witness stated for the first time on the 19th of May, and it's contained in this addendum. All of these allegations are very important for Major Sljivancanin. The people mentioned by this witness, as you were able to hear in today's testimony of this witness, all of this reflects on the relations between these people and Mr. Sljivancanin. As this witness is planned to testify tomorrow as well, we would like to ask you to allow us to consult Mr. Sljivancanin during the break and today so that we can start cross-examining this witness first thing in the morning. We believe that our cross-examination would take an hour to an hour and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any submission, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The addendum does not deal with Sljivancanin. It does deal with people who are linked to him. In our submission, it's a matter for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And it can be accommodated in your timetable for the week?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I wouldn't see any difficulty on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You must be owed a favour, Mr. Bulatovic. Yes, we will adjourn now, and we will resume tomorrow at -- if I could remind you, it must be at 12.30 tomorrow. We must sit tomorrow from 12.30 until 5.00, as we were planning to do today. Thursday and Friday it will be from 9.00 until 1.45. So we will adjourn now for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We will try to pay you back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 7th day of June, 2006, at 12.30 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.45 p.m.,
